reader: fresh agent (Claude Sonnet, no tools, no context), 2026-11-02, narration of research/library/drafts/story-myeongnyang.md v2 with the comedy ending and the 'one line' hook

hook.question_in_my_head: What was the one line, and how did thirteen ships beat a hundred and thirty-three?
hook.why: The 13 vs 133 mismatch plus the promised mystery line makes me want the payoff. 'Told to give up the navy' is a bit vague, and I don't know who Admiral Yi is.

who.Admiral Yi: Korean admiral who refuses to give up the navy; picks a narrow strait to fight in.
who.The king: Tells Yi to give up the navy because he thinks Yi has nothing left.
who.Yi's captains: Think he is mad, hang back and let him go first; after the win they eagerly follow him.
who.Japanese invasion fleet: Huge fleet (133 ships) that has already destroyed Korea's navy and wants to push through the strait.

what_happened: The king tells Yi to give up the navy, and Yi replies 'I still have ships.'
Yi has 13 ships left; the Japanese fleet of 133 fills the horizon.
Yi chooses a very narrow strait with a loud, rushing current to fight in.
The Japanese fleet is carried into the strait by the rushing water.
Yi's captains hang back and let him go first.
Only a few Japanese ships can reach Yi at a time, and his cannons hold them off.
The tide stops and reverses mid-battle.
The water flows back out, shoving the front Japanese ships into the ships behind them, and the tangle is stuck in front of Yi's cannons.
31 Japanese ships are lost, none of Yi's, and the rest turn back.
The captains now eagerly follow Yi.
why: The strait is so narrow that the big fleet can't use its numbers. The tide reversed partway through the battle, so the current that carried the Japanese in pushed them back into each other, jamming them in front of Yi's cannons. Yi picked the place and the tide did the rest.
twist: The king thought Yi had nothing left, but the strait and the tide, which turned and switched sides, were his real advantage.

ending.which_line_is_a_joke: 'Suddenly, his captains can't wait to follow him' (a dry joke on their earlier cowardice); the closing line is a punchline-style flourish
